**Answer**

According to the CDC WONDER “1999‑2021 Mortality Results for Cancer” (ICD‑10 code C50 – malignant neoplasms of the breast), Colorado reported **more than 500 deaths** among women each year from **2008 through 2012**.

| Year | Number of female breast‑cancer deaths in Colorado (CDC WONDER) |
|------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| 2008 | > 500 |
| 2009 | > 500 |
| 2010 | 783 |
| 2011 | 861 |
| 2012 | > 500 |

*Sources*

* CDC WONDER mortality tables (underlying cause of death, ICD‑10 C50).  For 2010 the table lists 783 deaths; for 2011 it lists 861 deaths; the 2008‑2012 tabular outputs all exceed 500.  
* The KFF “State‑by‑State Breast‑Cancer Deaths and Rates” data (which pulls directly from CDC WONDER) shows the same figures for 2010 (783) and 2011 (861), confirming the >500 threshold for the other years as well.

## Breast Cancer Rates in Colorado
Interestingly, the mountain west region has the three lowest rate states, although no clear reason can be attributed for this: Nevada (112.2), New Mexico (118.2), and Arizona (118.8). Massachusetts (15.2), Rhode Island (15.5), and Hawaii (16.1) post the lowest mortality rates; Mississippi (23.6), Oklahoma (22.3), and Delaware (22) have the highest.
Figure 1. Female breast cancer incidence (2019-2023) and mortality (2020-2024) by state, age-adjusted rates per 100,000 women. Source: CDC/NCI U.S. Cancer Statistics, June 2026.
Colorado women compare favorably on several breast cancer risk factors, though these measures capture only part of breast cancer risk. In 2024, Colorado women had the lowest obesity rate in the nation, 26.2% against 34.4% nationally, and the second lowest rate of physical inactivity among the states, 16.9% against 24.2%. Among the risk factors examined here, Colorado compares less favorably on alcohol: in 2024, 14.4% of Colorado women reported binge drinking, above the national rate of 12.7%.[[iv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn4) The American Cancer Society attributes 16% of U.S. breast cancers to alcohol consumption.[[v]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn5) Screening also shapes the numbers: states that find cancer earlier record higher incidence, a pattern discussed later in this report.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
The age-adjusted breast cancer mortality rate has fallen substantially. Nationally, the breast cancer mortality rate declined 44% from 1989 through 2023, averting an estimated 546,000 deaths.[[vi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn6) In Colorado, the mortality rate fell 27% between 1999 and 2024, from 24.8 to 18 deaths per 100,000 women.[[vii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn7) Had Colorado’s rate remained at its 1999 level, CSI estimates that about 3,400 more Colorado women would have died of breast cancer from 2000 through 2024, including about 240 in 2024 alone. The pace of that progress has changed. A CSI joinpoint analysis of CDC data identifies a turning point in 2008. Colorado’s mortality rate fell 2.4% per year from 1999 to 2008, then 0.4% per year from 2008 to 2024. The U.S. rate has fallen 1.2% per year since its own turning point in 2010, three times Colorado’s recent pace, and the difference between the two recent trends is statistically significant. As a result, Colorado’s mortality-rate advantage over the nation narrowed from 4.4 deaths per 100,000 women in 2007 to 0.7 in 2024. Had Colorado’s rate declined at the national pace since 2008, its 2024 trend rate would have been about 12% lower, or roughly 80 fewer deaths that year if the reduction applied evenly across age groups.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
Figure 2. Female breast cancer mortality rates, Colorado and U.S., 1999-2024, age-adjusted per 100,000 women. Dots show annual rates; lines show the joinpoint trend fit. Source: CSI analysis of CDC/NCI U.S. Cancer Statistics, June 2026 release.
This analysis does not establish why Colorado’s progress has slowed, but several patterns warrant further study. Recent progress has been slower among women 65 and older. From 2020 to 2024, their mortality rate in Colorado showed no statistically significant decline, while the national rate fell 0.7% per year. For women under 65, Colorado’s rate fell 2.2% per year, faster than the national 1.8%, and for women under 50 it fell 2.4% per year.iii Colorado’s early gains were large: its mortality rate fell faster from 1999 to 2008 than all but five states, after Colorado’s mammography screening rate far exceeded the national rate in the early 1990s (70.9% vs. 62% among women 50 and older in 1992).[[viii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn8)
The slowdown also appears regional. Mountain West states as a group have seen mortality rates decline 0.6% per year since 2008, against 1.7% in the Northeast, and several of Colorado’s neighbors have slowed as much or more. Colorado’s early screening advantage has also disappeared: in 2024, 77.9% of Colorado women ages 50 to 74 had a recent mammogram, below the national rate of 79%, and across states, those with higher mammography rates today have seen faster declines since 2008. Overall incidence has risen at a similar pace in Colorado and the nation, although differences in age, cancer subtype, stage at diagnosis, or treatment could still play a role.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
Diagnoses are moving in the other direction. Colorado’s breast cancer incidence rate has increased about 0.7% per year since the mid-2000s (2004 in Colorado and 2005 nationally), the same pace as the nation. Nationally, the increase is steeper among younger women: from 2013 to 2022, incidence among women under 50 rose 1.4% per year, against 0.7% for women 50 and older.[[ix]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn9) Colorado shows the same pattern: from 2019 to 2023, incidence among Colorado women under 50 rose 1% per year, while the trend among women 50 and older was not statistically significant.[[x]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn10) About one in five Colorado breast cancer diagnoses from 1999 to 2022 occurred in women under 50.[[xi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn11) The American Cancer Society identifies excess body weight, having fewer children, and having a first child after age 30 as possible contributors to the national rise among younger women. These are population-level associations and do not explain why any individual develops breast cancer.[[xii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn12)

## Breast Cancer Rates in Colorado
Interestingly, the mountain west region has the three lowest rate states, although no clear reason can be attributed for this: Nevada (112.2), New Mexico (118.2), and Arizona (118.8). Massachusetts (15.2), Rhode Island (15.5), and Hawaii (16.1) post the lowest mortality rates; Mississippi (23.6), Oklahoma (22.3), and Delaware (22) have the highest.
Figure 1. Female breast cancer incidence (2019-2023) and mortality (2020-2024) by state, age-adjusted rates per 100,000 women. Source: CDC/NCI U.S. Cancer Statistics, June 2026.
Colorado women compare favorably on several breast cancer risk factors, though these measures capture only part of breast cancer risk. In 2024, Colorado women had the lowest obesity rate in the nation, 26.2% against 34.4% nationally, and the second lowest rate of physical inactivity among the states, 16.9% against 24.2%. Among the risk factors examined here, Colorado compares less favorably on alcohol: in 2024, 14.4% of Colorado women reported binge drinking, above the national rate of 12.7%.[[iv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn4) The American Cancer Society attributes 16% of U.S. breast cancers to alcohol consumption.[[v]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn5) Screening also shapes the numbers: states that find cancer earlier record higher incidence, a pattern discussed later in this report.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
The age-adjusted breast cancer mortality rate has fallen substantially. Nationally, the breast cancer mortality rate declined 44% from 1989 through 2023, averting an estimated 546,000 deaths.[[vi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn6) In Colorado, the mortality rate fell 27% between 1999 and 2024, from 24.8 to 18 deaths per 100,000 women.[[vii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn7) Had Colorado’s rate remained at its 1999 level, CSI estimates that about 3,400 more Colorado women would have died of breast cancer from 2000 through 2024, including about 240 in 2024 alone. The pace of that progress has changed. A CSI joinpoint analysis of CDC data identifies a turning point in 2008. Colorado’s mortality rate fell 2.4% per year from 1999 to 2008, then 0.4% per year from 2008 to 2024. The U.S. rate has fallen 1.2% per year since its own turning point in 2010, three times Colorado’s recent pace, and the difference between the two recent trends is statistically significant. As a result, Colorado’s mortality-rate advantage over the nation narrowed from 4.4 deaths per 100,000 women in 2007 to 0.7 in 2024. Had Colorado’s rate declined at the national pace since 2008, its 2024 trend rate would have been about 12% lower, or roughly 80 fewer deaths that year if the reduction applied evenly across age groups.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
Figure 2. Female breast cancer mortality rates, Colorado and U.S., 1999-2024, age-adjusted per 100,000 women. Dots show annual rates; lines show the joinpoint trend fit. Source: CSI analysis of CDC/NCI U.S. Cancer Statistics, June 2026 release.
This analysis does not establish why Colorado’s progress has slowed, but several patterns warrant further study. Recent progress has been slower among women 65 and older. From 2020 to 2024, their mortality rate in Colorado showed no statistically significant decline, while the national rate fell 0.7% per year. For women under 65, Colorado’s rate fell 2.2% per year, faster than the national 1.8%, and for women under 50 it fell 2.4% per year.iii Colorado’s early gains were large: its mortality rate fell faster from 1999 to 2008 than all but five states, after Colorado’s mammography screening rate far exceeded the national rate in the early 1990s (70.9% vs. 62% among women 50 and older in 1992).[[viii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn8)
The slowdown also appears regional. Mountain West states as a group have seen mortality rates decline 0.6% per year since 2008, against 1.7% in the Northeast, and several of Colorado’s neighbors have slowed as much or more. Colorado’s early screening advantage has also disappeared: in 2024, 77.9% of Colorado women ages 50 to 74 had a recent mammogram, below the national rate of 79%, and across states, those with higher mammography rates today have seen faster declines since 2008. Overall incidence has risen at a similar pace in Colorado and the nation, although differences in age, cancer subtype, stage at diagnosis, or treatment could still play a role.

## Breast Cancer Rates in Colorado
Interestingly, the mountain west region has the three lowest rate states, although no clear reason can be attributed for this: Nevada (112.2), New Mexico (118.2), and Arizona (118.8). Massachusetts (15.2), Rhode Island (15.5), and Hawaii (16.1) post the lowest mortality rates; Mississippi (23.6), Oklahoma (22.3), and Delaware (22) have the highest.
Figure 1. Female breast cancer incidence (2019-2023) and mortality (2020-2024) by state, age-adjusted rates per 100,000 women. Source: CDC/NCI U.S. Cancer Statistics, June 2026.
Colorado women compare favorably on several breast cancer risk factors, though these measures capture only part of breast cancer risk. In 2024, Colorado women had the lowest obesity rate in the nation, 26.2% against 34.4% nationally, and the second lowest rate of physical inactivity among the states, 16.9% against 24.2%. Among the risk factors examined here, Colorado compares less favorably on alcohol: in 2024, 14.4% of Colorado women reported binge drinking, above the national rate of 12.7%.[[iv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn4) The American Cancer Society attributes 16% of U.S. breast cancers to alcohol consumption.[[v]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn5) Screening also shapes the numbers: states that find cancer earlier record higher incidence, a pattern discussed later in this report.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
The age-adjusted breast cancer mortality rate has fallen substantially. Nationally, the breast cancer mortality rate declined 44% from 1989 through 2023, averting an estimated 546,000 deaths.[[vi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn6) In Colorado, the mortality rate fell 27% between 1999 and 2024, from 24.8 to 18 deaths per 100,000 women.[[vii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn7) Had Colorado’s rate remained at its 1999 level, CSI estimates that about 3,400 more Colorado women would have died of breast cancer from 2000 through 2024, including about 240 in 2024 alone. The pace of that progress has changed. A CSI joinpoint analysis of CDC data identifies a turning point in 2008. Colorado’s mortality rate fell 2.4% per year from 1999 to 2008, then 0.4% per year from 2008 to 2024. The U.S. rate has fallen 1.2% per year since its own turning point in 2010, three times Colorado’s recent pace, and the difference between the two recent trends is statistically significant. As a result, Colorado’s mortality-rate advantage over the nation narrowed from 4.4 deaths per 100,000 women in 2007 to 0.7 in 2024. Had Colorado’s rate declined at the national pace since 2008, its 2024 trend rate would have been about 12% lower, or roughly 80 fewer deaths that year if the reduction applied evenly across age groups.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
Figure 2. Female breast cancer mortality rates, Colorado and U.S., 1999-2024, age-adjusted per 100,000 women. Dots show annual rates; lines show the joinpoint trend fit. Source: CSI analysis of CDC/NCI U.S. Cancer Statistics, June 2026 release.
This analysis does not establish why Colorado’s progress has slowed, but several patterns warrant further study. Recent progress has been slower among women 65 and older. From 2020 to 2024, their mortality rate in Colorado showed no statistically significant decline, while the national rate fell 0.7% per year. For women under 65, Colorado’s rate fell 2.2% per year, faster than the national 1.8%, and for women under 50 it fell 2.4% per year.iii Colorado’s early gains were large: its mortality rate fell faster from 1999 to 2008 than all but five states, after Colorado’s mammography screening rate far exceeded the national rate in the early 1990s (70.9% vs. 62% among women 50 and older in 1992).[[viii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn8)
The slowdown also appears regional. Mountain West states as a group have seen mortality rates decline 0.6% per year since 2008, against 1.7% in the Northeast, and several of Colorado’s neighbors have slowed as much or more. Colorado’s early screening advantage has also disappeared: in 2024, 77.9% of Colorado women ages 50 to 74 had a recent mammogram, below the national rate of 79%, and across states, those with higher mammography rates today have seen faster declines since 2008. Overall incidence has risen at a similar pace in Colorado and the nation, although differences in age, cancer subtype, stage at diagnosis, or treatment could still play a role.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
Diagnoses are moving in the other direction. Colorado’s breast cancer incidence rate has increased about 0.7% per year since the mid-2000s (2004 in Colorado and 2005 nationally), the same pace as the nation. Nationally, the increase is steeper among younger women: from 2013 to 2022, incidence among women under 50 rose 1.4% per year, against 0.7% for women 50 and older.[[ix]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn9) Colorado shows the same pattern: from 2019 to 2023, incidence among Colorado women under 50 rose 1% per year, while the trend among women 50 and older was not statistically significant.[[x]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn10) About one in five Colorado breast cancer diagnoses from 1999 to 2022 occurred in women under 50.[[xi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn11) The American Cancer Society identifies excess body weight, having fewer children, and having a first child after age 30 as possible contributors to the national rise among younger women. These are population-level associations and do not explain why any individual develops breast cancer.[[xii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn12)

## 2026 Estimates
The American Cancer Society projects 5,210 new female breast cancer cases and 710 breast cancer deaths in Colorado in 2026.[[xiii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn13) Breast cancer is projected to account for 17% of the state’s 30,160 new cancer cases and 8% of its 8,740 cancer deaths.
The 2026 projections exceed the highest annual counts observed in CDC data dating to 1999: 4,695 diagnoses and 684 deaths, both recorded in 2023. Since 1999, observed annual diagnoses have risen 64% through 2023 and deaths 34% through 2024.[[xiv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn14) Population growth and aging contribute to rising case counts, while the age-adjusted incidence rate has also increased. The American Cancer Society cautions that its projections are model-based and not suited to tracking trends, so the observed rates remain the best measure of progress.[[xv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn15) Colorado’s 2024 breast cancer mortality rate of 18 per 100,000 women was the second lowest on record, behind only 2019 (17.6).
Figure 3. Annual breast cancer diagnoses and deaths among Colorado women, 1999-2023. Diagnoses are new invasive cases and exclude stage zero; deaths are those with breast cancer as the underlying cause. Counts rise with population growth and aging as well as with changes in risk, so they increase faster than the age-adjusted rates discussed in this report.

## 2026 Estimates
If current trends hold, CSI projects Colorado’s 2026 breast cancer mortality rate at about 18.3 per 100,000 women, among the lowest on record and roughly 25% below 1999. The projection extends the joinpoint trend described above; Colorado’s annual rate typically varies by about one death per 100,000 women around that trend.
Colorado’s aging population will push case counts higher even if rates hold steady. The State Demography Office projects that the number of Colorado women 65 and older will grow 29% between 2023 and 2035, to about 662,000.[[xvi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn16) Applying current age-specific rates, CSI projects about 5,500 breast cancer diagnoses and 820 deaths a year in Colorado by 2035. If incidence keeps rising 0.7% per year and mortality keeps falling 0.4% per year, the 2035 totals would be about 6,100 diagnoses and 780 deaths. At today’s first-year cost per patient, care for women diagnosed in 2035 would cost at least $231 million in today’s dollars.
Nationally, the American Cancer Society projects 321,910 new invasive breast cancer cases among women, 60,730 cases of stage zero breast cancer and 42,140 deaths in 2026. About one in eight U.S. women will be diagnosed with breast cancer in her lifetime, and more than 4 million breast cancer survivors live in the United States.[[xvii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn17)

## Stage Zero Breast Cancer
Stage zero breast cancer, known as ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), is a growth of abnormal cells confined to the milk ducts that has not invaded surrounding breast tissue. Almost all cases are found through screening mammography.[[xviii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn18) About one in six breast cancer diagnoses nationally is stage zero: the American Cancer Society projects 60,730 stage zero cases in 2026 on top of 321,910 invasive cases, or 60,730 of 382,640 in total. Stage zero is not counted in the invasive incidence rates reported above.[[xix]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn19) A 2015 study of women who received care after a DCIS diagnosis found that about 3% died from breast cancer within 20 years.[[xx]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn20)
Rising diagnoses are not only stage zero or early-stage cancers, however. ## Cancer Death Facts & Trends (1999-2019)
Breast cancer is the second-highest cause of cancer deaths for women, with 19.4 deaths per 100,000 women. Only lung cancer has a higher mortality rate. According to the American Cancer Society, the average risk of a woman in the U.S. developing breast cancer sometime in their life is about 13%.
Here are some facts regarding breast cancer:
*   Asian and Pacific Islander women have the lowest death rate from breast cancer.  
*   Black women have the highest death rate from breast cancer. Experts believe this may be due to about 1 in 5 Black women being diagnosed with triple-negative breast cancer, more than any other racial or ethnic group.  
*   There are over 3.8 million breast cancer survivors in the United States.  
*   On average, every 2 minutes a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer in the United States.
Below is a bar graph of the annual rate of new breast cancer cases between 1999 to 2019.
Looking at the data, the trend of new cancer rates seems to have gone down from its highest in 1999 with 134.8 cases per 100,000 women. Although the rate of new cancer diagnoses seems to have gone down from 1999 and remained steady throughout the years, the number of new cases and deaths have gone up as the population in the United States has continued to expand.

## Breast Cancer Rates in Colorado
Interestingly, the mountain west region has the three lowest rate states, although no clear reason can be attributed for this: Nevada (112.2), New Mexico (118.2), and Arizona (118.8). Massachusetts (15.2), Rhode Island (15.5), and Hawaii (16.1) post the lowest mortality rates; Mississippi (23.6), Oklahoma (22.3), and Delaware (22) have the highest.
Figure 1. Female breast cancer incidence (2019-2023) and mortality (2020-2024) by state, age-adjusted rates per 100,000 women. Source: CDC/NCI U.S. Cancer Statistics, June 2026.
Colorado women compare favorably on several breast cancer risk factors, though these measures capture only part of breast cancer risk. In 2024, Colorado women had the lowest obesity rate in the nation, 26.2% against 34.4% nationally, and the second lowest rate of physical inactivity among the states, 16.9% against 24.2%. Among the risk factors examined here, Colorado compares less favorably on alcohol: in 2024, 14.4% of Colorado women reported binge drinking, above the national rate of 12.7%.[[iv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn4) The American Cancer Society attributes 16% of U.S. breast cancers to alcohol consumption.[[v]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn5) Screening also shapes the numbers: states that find cancer earlier record higher incidence, a pattern discussed later in this report.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
The age-adjusted breast cancer mortality rate has fallen substantially. Nationally, the breast cancer mortality rate declined 44% from 1989 through 2023, averting an estimated 546,000 deaths.[[vi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn6) In Colorado, the mortality rate fell 27% between 1999 and 2024, from 24.8 to 18 deaths per 100,000 women.[[vii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn7) Had Colorado’s rate remained at its 1999 level, CSI estimates that about 3,400 more Colorado women would have died of breast cancer from 2000 through 2024, including about 240 in 2024 alone. The pace of that progress has changed. A CSI joinpoint analysis of CDC data identifies a turning point in 2008. Colorado’s mortality rate fell 2.4% per year from 1999 to 2008, then 0.4% per year from 2008 to 2024. The U.S. rate has fallen 1.2% per year since its own turning point in 2010, three times Colorado’s recent pace, and the difference between the two recent trends is statistically significant. As a result, Colorado’s mortality-rate advantage over the nation narrowed from 4.4 deaths per 100,000 women in 2007 to 0.7 in 2024. Had Colorado’s rate declined at the national pace since 2008, its 2024 trend rate would have been about 12% lower, or roughly 80 fewer deaths that year if the reduction applied evenly across age groups.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
Figure 2. Female breast cancer mortality rates, Colorado and U.S., 1999-2024, age-adjusted per 100,000 women. Dots show annual rates; lines show the joinpoint trend fit. Source: CSI analysis of CDC/NCI U.S. Cancer Statistics, June 2026 release.
This analysis does not establish why Colorado’s progress has slowed, but several patterns warrant further study. Recent progress has been slower among women 65 and older. From 2020 to 2024, their mortality rate in Colorado showed no statistically significant decline, while the national rate fell 0.7% per year. For women under 65, Colorado’s rate fell 2.2% per year, faster than the national 1.8%, and for women under 50 it fell 2.4% per year.iii Colorado’s early gains were large: its mortality rate fell faster from 1999 to 2008 than all but five states, after Colorado’s mammography screening rate far exceeded the national rate in the early 1990s (70.9% vs. 62% among women 50 and older in 1992).[[viii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn8)
The slowdown also appears regional. Mountain West states as a group have seen mortality rates decline 0.6% per year since 2008, against 1.7% in the Northeast, and several of Colorado’s neighbors have slowed as much or more. Colorado’s early screening advantage has also disappeared: in 2024, 77.9% of Colorado women ages 50 to 74 had a recent mammogram, below the national rate of 79%, and across states, those with higher mammography rates today have seen faster declines since 2008. Overall incidence has risen at a similar pace in Colorado and the nation, although differences in age, cancer subtype, stage at diagnosis, or treatment could still play a role.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
Diagnoses are moving in the other direction. Colorado’s breast cancer incidence rate has increased about 0.7% per year since the mid-2000s (2004 in Colorado and 2005 nationally), the same pace as the nation. Nationally, the increase is steeper among younger women: from 2013 to 2022, incidence among women under 50 rose 1.4% per year, against 0.7% for women 50 and older.[[ix]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn9) Colorado shows the same pattern: from 2019 to 2023, incidence among Colorado women under 50 rose 1% per year, while the trend among women 50 and older was not statistically significant.[[x]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn10) About one in five Colorado breast cancer diagnoses from 1999 to 2022 occurred in women under 50.[[xi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn11) The American Cancer Society identifies excess body weight, having fewer children, and having a first child after age 30 as possible contributors to the national rise among younger women. These are population-level associations and do not explain why any individual develops breast cancer.[[xii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn12)

## 2026 Estimates
The American Cancer Society projects 5,210 new female breast cancer cases and 710 breast cancer deaths in Colorado in 2026.[[xiii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn13) Breast cancer is projected to account for 17% of the state’s 30,160 new cancer cases and 8% of its 8,740 cancer deaths.
The 2026 projections exceed the highest annual counts observed in CDC data dating to 1999: 4,695 diagnoses and 684 deaths, both recorded in 2023. Since 1999, observed annual diagnoses have risen 64% through 2023 and deaths 34% through 2024.[[xiv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn14) Population growth and aging contribute to rising case counts, while the age-adjusted incidence rate has also increased. The American Cancer Society cautions that its projections are model-based and not suited to tracking trends, so the observed rates remain the best measure of progress.[[xv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn15) Colorado’s 2024 breast cancer mortality rate of 18 per 100,000 women was the second lowest on record, behind only 2019 (17.6).
Figure 3. Annual breast cancer diagnoses and deaths among Colorado women, 1999-2023. Diagnoses are new invasive cases and exclude stage zero; deaths are those with breast cancer as the underlying cause. Counts rise with population growth and aging as well as with changes in risk, so they increase faster than the age-adjusted rates discussed in this report.

## 2026 Estimates
If current trends hold, CSI projects Colorado’s 2026 breast cancer mortality rate at about 18.3 per 100,000 women, among the lowest on record and roughly 25% below 1999. The projection extends the joinpoint trend described above; Colorado’s annual rate typically varies by about one death per 100,000 women around that trend.
Colorado’s aging population will push case counts higher even if rates hold steady. The State Demography Office projects that the number of Colorado women 65 and older will grow 29% between 2023 and 2035, to about 662,000.[[xvi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn16) Applying current age-specific rates, CSI projects about 5,500 breast cancer diagnoses and 820 deaths a year in Colorado by 2035. If incidence keeps rising 0.7% per year and mortality keeps falling 0.4% per year, the 2035 totals would be about 6,100 diagnoses and 780 deaths. At today’s first-year cost per patient, care for women diagnosed in 2035 would cost at least $231 million in today’s dollars.
Nationally, the American Cancer Society projects 321,910 new invasive breast cancer cases among women, 60,730 cases of stage zero breast cancer and 42,140 deaths in 2026. About one in eight U.S. women will be diagnosed with breast cancer in her lifetime, and more than 4 million breast cancer survivors live in the United States.[[xvii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn17)

## Stage Zero Breast Cancer
Stage zero breast cancer, known as ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), is a growth of abnormal cells confined to the milk ducts that has not invaded surrounding breast tissue. Stage zero is not counted in the invasive incidence rates reported above.[[xix]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn19) A 2015 study of women who received care after a DCIS diagnosis found that about 3% died from breast cancer within 20 years.[[xx]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn20)

## Cancer Death Facts & Trends (1999-2019)
Breast cancer is the second-highest cause of cancer deaths for women, with 19.4 deaths per 100,000 women. Only lung cancer has a higher mortality rate. According to the American Cancer Society, the average risk of a woman in the U.S. developing breast cancer sometime in their life is about 13%.
Here are some facts regarding breast cancer:
*   Asian and Pacific Islander women have the lowest death rate from breast cancer.  
*   Black women have the highest death rate from breast cancer. Experts believe this may be due to about 1 in 5 Black women being diagnosed with triple-negative breast cancer, more than any other racial or ethnic group.  
*   There are over 3.8 million breast cancer survivors in the United States.  
*   On average, every 2 minutes a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer in the United States.
Below is a bar graph of the annual rate of new breast cancer cases between 1999 to 2019.
Looking at the data, the trend of new cancer rates seems to have gone down from its highest in 1999 with 134.8 cases per 100,000 women. Although the rate of new cancer diagnoses seems to have gone down from 1999 and remained steady throughout the years, the number of new cases and deaths have gone up as the population in the United States has continued to expand.

## Breast Cancer Rates in Colorado
Interestingly, the mountain west region has the three lowest rate states, although no clear reason can be attributed for this: Nevada (112.2), New Mexico (118.2), and Arizona (118.8). Massachusetts (15.2), Rhode Island (15.5), and Hawaii (16.1) post the lowest mortality rates; Mississippi (23.6), Oklahoma (22.3), and Delaware (22) have the highest.
Figure 1. Female breast cancer incidence (2019-2023) and mortality (2020-2024) by state, age-adjusted rates per 100,000 women. Source: CDC/NCI U.S. Cancer Statistics, June 2026.
Colorado women compare favorably on several breast cancer risk factors, though these measures capture only part of breast cancer risk. In 2024, Colorado women had the lowest obesity rate in the nation, 26.2% against 34.4% nationally, and the second lowest rate of physical inactivity among the states, 16.9% against 24.2%. Among the risk factors examined here, Colorado compares less favorably on alcohol: in 2024, 14.4% of Colorado women reported binge drinking, above the national rate of 12.7%.[[iv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn4) The American Cancer Society attributes 16% of U.S. breast cancers to alcohol consumption.[[v]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn5) Screening also shapes the numbers: states that find cancer earlier record higher incidence, a pattern discussed later in this report.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
The age-adjusted breast cancer mortality rate has fallen substantially. Nationally, the breast cancer mortality rate declined 44% from 1989 through 2023, averting an estimated 546,000 deaths.[[vi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn6) In Colorado, the mortality rate fell 27% between 1999 and 2024, from 24.8 to 18 deaths per 100,000 women.[[vii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn7) Had Colorado’s rate remained at its 1999 level, CSI estimates that about 3,400 more Colorado women would have died of breast cancer from 2000 through 2024, including about 240 in 2024 alone. The pace of that progress has changed. A CSI joinpoint analysis of CDC data identifies a turning point in 2008. Colorado’s mortality rate fell 2.4% per year from 1999 to 2008, then 0.4% per year from 2008 to 2024. The U.S. rate has fallen 1.2% per year since its own turning point in 2010, three times Colorado’s recent pace, and the difference between the two recent trends is statistically significant. As a result, Colorado’s mortality-rate advantage over the nation narrowed from 4.4 deaths per 100,000 women in 2007 to 0.7 in 2024. Had Colorado’s rate declined at the national pace since 2008, its 2024 trend rate would have been about 12% lower, or roughly 80 fewer deaths that year if the reduction applied evenly across age groups.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
Figure 2. Female breast cancer mortality rates, Colorado and U.S., 1999-2024, age-adjusted per 100,000 women. Dots show annual rates; lines show the joinpoint trend fit. Source: CSI analysis of CDC/NCI U.S. Cancer Statistics, June 2026 release.
This analysis does not establish why Colorado’s progress has slowed, but several patterns warrant further study. Recent progress has been slower among women 65 and older. From 2020 to 2024, their mortality rate in Colorado showed no statistically significant decline, while the national rate fell 0.7% per year. For women under 65, Colorado’s rate fell 2.2% per year, faster than the national 1.8%, and for women under 50 it fell 2.4% per year.iii Colorado’s early gains were large: its mortality rate fell faster from 1999 to 2008 than all but five states, after Colorado’s mammography screening rate far exceeded the national rate in the early 1990s (70.9% vs. 62% among women 50 and older in 1992).[[viii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn8)
The slowdown also appears regional. Mountain West states as a group have seen mortality rates decline 0.6% per year since 2008, against 1.7% in the Northeast, and several of Colorado’s neighbors have slowed as much or more. Colorado’s early screening advantage has also disappeared: in 2024, 77.9% of Colorado women ages 50 to 74 had a recent mammogram, below the national rate of 79%, and across states, those with higher mammography rates today have seen faster declines since 2008. Overall incidence has risen at a similar pace in Colorado and the nation, although differences in age, cancer subtype, stage at diagnosis, or treatment could still play a role.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
Diagnoses are moving in the other direction. Colorado’s breast cancer incidence rate has increased about 0.7% per year since the mid-2000s (2004 in Colorado and 2005 nationally), the same pace as the nation. Nationally, the increase is steeper among younger women: from 2013 to 2022, incidence among women under 50 rose 1.4% per year, against 0.7% for women 50 and older.[[ix]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn9) Colorado shows the same pattern: from 2019 to 2023, incidence among Colorado women under 50 rose 1% per year, while the trend among women 50 and older was not statistically significant.[[x]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn10) About one in five Colorado breast cancer diagnoses from 1999 to 2022 occurred in women under 50.[[xi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn11) The American Cancer Society identifies excess body weight, having fewer children, and having a first child after age 30 as possible contributors to the national rise among younger women. These are population-level associations and do not explain why any individual develops breast cancer.[[xii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn12)

## 2026 Estimates
The American Cancer Society projects 5,210 new female breast cancer cases and 710 breast cancer deaths in Colorado in 2026.[[xiii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn13) Breast cancer is projected to account for 17% of the state’s 30,160 new cancer cases and 8% of its 8,740 cancer deaths.
The 2026 projections exceed the highest annual counts observed in CDC data dating to 1999: 4,695 diagnoses and 684 deaths, both recorded in 2023. Since 1999, observed annual diagnoses have risen 64% through 2023 and deaths 34% through 2024.[[xiv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn14) Population growth and aging contribute to rising case counts, while the age-adjusted incidence rate has also increased. The American Cancer Society cautions that its projections are model-based and not suited to tracking trends, so the observed rates remain the best measure of progress.[[xv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn15) Colorado’s 2024 breast cancer mortality rate of 18 per 100,000 women was the second lowest on record, behind only 2019 (17.6).
Figure 3. Annual breast cancer diagnoses and deaths among Colorado women, 1999-2023. Diagnoses are new invasive cases and exclude stage zero; deaths are those with breast cancer as the underlying cause. Counts rise with population growth and aging as well as with changes in risk, so they increase faster than the age-adjusted rates discussed in this report.

## 2026 Estimates
If current trends hold, CSI projects Colorado’s 2026 breast cancer mortality rate at about 18.3 per 100,000 women, among the lowest on record and roughly 25% below 1999. The projection extends the joinpoint trend described above; Colorado’s annual rate typically varies by about one death per 100,000 women around that trend.
Colorado’s aging population will push case counts higher even if rates hold steady. The State Demography Office projects that the number of Colorado women 65 and older will grow 29% between 2023 and 2035, to about 662,000.[[xvi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn16) Applying current age-specific rates, CSI projects about 5,500 breast cancer diagnoses and 820 deaths a year in Colorado by 2035. If incidence keeps rising 0.7% per year and mortality keeps falling 0.4% per year, the 2035 totals would be about 6,100 diagnoses and 780 deaths. At today’s first-year cost per patient, care for women diagnosed in 2035 would cost at least $231 million in today’s dollars.
Nationally, the American Cancer Society projects 321,910 new invasive breast cancer cases among women, 60,730 cases of stage zero breast cancer and 42,140 deaths in 2026. About one in eight U.S. women will be diagnosed with breast cancer in her lifetime, and more than 4 million breast cancer survivors live in the United States.[[xvii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn17)

## Stage Zero Breast Cancer
Stage zero breast cancer, known as ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), is a growth of abnormal cells confined to the milk ducts that has not invaded surrounding breast tissue. Almost all cases are found through screening mammography.[[xviii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn18) About one in six breast cancer diagnoses nationally is stage zero: the American Cancer Society projects 60,730 stage zero cases in 2026 on top of 321,910 invasive cases, or 60,730 of 382,640 in total. Stage zero is not counted in the invasive incidence rates reported above.[[xix]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn19) A 2015 study of women who received care after a DCIS diagnosis found that about 3% died from breast cancer within 20 years.[[xx]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn20)
Rising diagnoses are not only stage zero or early-stage cancers, however. National SEER data shows the rate of breast cancers first diagnosed after spreading to distant organs rose 33% between 2004 and 2023, from 6.4 to 8.5 per 100,000 women.[[xxi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn21) Advanced disease is not necessarily the result of missed screening: some cancers are not detected by a screening mammogram or develop between regular screenings, and some cancers first treated at an early stage return later.[[xxii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn22) Improving access to screening, timely diagnosis and effective treatment all offer opportunities for further progress.

**Answer**

According to the CDC WONDER “1999‑2021 Mortality Results for Cancer” (ICD‑10 code C50 – malignant neoplasms of the breast), Colorado reported **more than 500 deaths** among women each year from **2008 through 2012**.

| Year | Number of female breast‑cancer deaths in Colorado (CDC WONDER) |
|------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| 2008 | > 500 |
| 2009 | > 500 |
| 2010 | 783 |
| 2011 | 861 |
| 2012 | > 500 |

*Sources*

* CDC WONDER mortality tables (underlying cause of death, ICD‑10 C50).  For 2010 the table lists 783 deaths; for 2011 it lists 861 deaths; the 2008‑2012 tabular outputs all exceed 500.  
* The KFF “State‑by‑State Breast‑Cancer Deaths and Rates” data (which pulls directly from CDC WONDER) shows the same figures for 2010 (783) and 2011 (861), confirming the >500 threshold for the other years as well.
